paras: The lynching of Leonard Coker was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd of whites and blacks near Cowles Station, Alabama, about 30 miles east of Montgomery, on August 25, 1882. Coker was accused of outraging and murdering a white woman, most often named as Catharine Haynes, and was hanged to a tree at the scene of the alleged crime after a search and a reported confession. An Associated Press dispatch from Montgomery carried the story to papers across the country, several of which presented the killing as deserved.

According to the Montgomery dispatch, a woman named Cathrine Haynes was outraged and murdered on the Monday before the lynching, about 30 miles east of Montgomery on the Western railroad. The Huntsville Gazette, in its Alabama news column, described her as 'an aged white woman' and placed the events at Cowle's station. Her name appeared in many forms, including Hanes, Haines, Hayes, Hynes and Payne, and two briefs described her as being from Macon county, Tennessee.

A crowd of whites and blacks took part in the search for Coker, who was captured on the afternoon of Friday, August 25. The dispatch said he confessed 'as the evidence of his guilt was overwhelming', citing pieces of his clothing found near the scene and reports that he had been seen with the woman several times that day. The evidence and the confession are known only from this account, which treated his guilt as established.

After the capture the crowd carried Coker to the spot where the woman had been killed and hanged him to a tree until he was dead. The Huntsville Gazette dated the lynching to Friday night, August 25, and the Portland Daily Press and the Wilmington Daily Republican both called the killers 'a mob of blacks and whites'. No account mentions sheriffs, constables or any other officers.
No report of an inquest, an arrest of any member of the crowd, or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage.

The Associated Press dispatch, datelined Montgomery, August 26, appeared that day in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, the Washington Evening Star, the Alexandria Gazette and the Memphis Public Ledger, and on the following days in the New-York Tribune, the Memphis Daily Appeal, the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Portland Daily Press. Shorter versions spread west to Seattle, Sacramento, Cheyenne, Omaha and Elko, and syndicated digests carried it into weekly papers in Minnesota, Wisconsin, Kansas, Tennessee and Michigan into early September.

Headlines put the alleged crime first and often endorsed the killing: the Evening Star ran 'THE DESERVED FATE OF AN ALABAMA NEGRO', and the Omaha Daily Bee headed its special dispatch 'The Right Remedy'. Other papers used 'AVENGING A TERKIBLE CRIME', 'Quick Work Made With a Negro Murderer' and, in the Memphis Daily Appeal, 'A Black Fleud [Fiend] Hauged to a Tree', while the Seattle Post-Intelligencer used the slur 'Darkey Hung'. The Richmond Dispatch listed the story in its telegraphic index as 'An Alabama Negro Lynched for Rape', and a Michigan weekly ran it under 'GONE TO GAHENNA', calling Coker 'the villain'.

Nearly every version noted that the crowd was made up of both whites and blacks, and only the Alexandria Gazette described it as 'a crowd of infuriated persons'. In Alabama, the Huntsville Gazette ran both a two-line state-news item and the syndicated national digest in its September 2 issue.

Most accounts put the capture and lynching on Friday, August 25, but the Omaha Daily Bee's August 27 dispatch said Coker was captured 'yesterday', and the Elko Independent said he was hanged on Saturday. The Friday date has the better support, since it comes from the first-day dispatch and the Alabama item.

Two paragraph-news columns, in the Hickman Courier and the Rock Island Argus, reported that the woman near Cowles Station had been outraged and murdered 'by tramps', without naming Coker or mentioning a lynching.

reader.title: Lynching of Leonard Coker
bases: A crowd that had hunted Leonard Coker as the accused in the rape and murder of a white woman hanged him to a tree at the scene of the crime (A3, A4, A23).

Every account says Coker was hanged until dead by a crowd or mob, with no officers or legal process reported (A3, A15, A23); the stated reason was punishment for the alleged outrage and murder, and the Evening Star called it his 'deserved fate' (A4, A8).

The Associated Press dispatch from Montgomery (A3, A4, A9) is matched on the core event by a separate Alabama state-news item in the Huntsville Gazette (A23) and a syndicated item naming Cowles Station (A19); two briefs blaming 'tramps' concern who committed the crime, not the lynching (A21, A27).

framing.detail: The Evening Star headed the wire 'THE DESERVED FATE OF AN ALABAMA NEGRO' and the Omaha Daily Bee headed its special 'The Right Remedy'.

Headlines stressed the crowd and the crime, such as 'AVENGING A TERKIBLE CRIME', 'A Negro Hung to a Tree by an Infuriated Mob' and 'Quick Work Made With a Negro Murderer', while the text called Coker's guilt 'overwhelming'.
Most papers ran the Montgomery wire or a syndicated digest of it without comment, some only as one line.
